blocks.html:
The Placebo Effect

With the right encouragement, your mind can convince the body to heal itself. What is the mysterious force that can do this?

Want to devise a new form of alternative medical treatment? No problem. Here's the recipe. As a practitioner, be warm, sympathetic, reassuring and enthusiastic. Your treatment should involve physical contact, and each session with your patients should take at least half an hour. Encourage your patients to take an active part in their treatment and understand how their disorders relate to the rest of their lives. Tell them that their own bodies possess the true power to heal. Get them to pay you well. Describe your treatment in familiar words, but embroidered with a hint of mysticism: energy fields, energy flows, energy blocks, meridians, forces, auras, rhythms and the like. Refer to the knowledge of an earlier age: wisdom carelessly swept aside by the rise of blind mechanistic science. Oh, come off it, you're saying. Something like that couldn't possibly work, could it?

Well, yes, it could and often well enough to earn you a living. And a very good living if you are sufficiently convincing or, better still, really believe in your therapy. Many illnesses get better on their own, so if you are lucky and administer your treatment at just the right time you'll get the credit. But that's only part of it. Some of the improvement really would be down to you. Not necessarily because you'd recommended ginseng rather than chamomile tea or used this crystal as opposed to that pressure point. Nothing so specific. Your healing power would be the outcome of a paradoxical force that conventional medicine recognizes but remains oddly ambivalent about: the placebo effect.

Placebos are treatments that have no direct effect on the body, yet still work because the patient has faith in their power to heal. Most often the term refers to a dummy pill, but it applies just as much to any device or procedure, from a sticking plaster to a crystal. The existence of the placebo effect implies that even a complete fraud could make a difference to someone's health, which is why some practitioners of alternative medicine are sensitive about any mention of the subject. In fact, the placebo is a powerful part of all medical care, orthodox or otherwise, though its role is often neglected and misunderstood.

At one level, it should come as no surprise that our state of mind can influence our physiology: anger opens the superficial blood vessels of the face; sadness pumps the tear glands. But exactly how placebos work their medical magic is still largely unknown. Most of the scant research to date has focused on the control of pain, because it's one of the commonest complaints and lends itself to experimental study. Here, attention has turned to the endorphins, natural substances produced in the brain that are known to help control pain. Any of the neurochemicals involved in transmitting pain impulses or modulating them might also be involved in generating the placebo response, says Don Price, an oral surgeon at the University of Florida.

That case has been strengthened by the recent work of Fabrizio Benedetti of the University of Turin, who showed that the placebo effect can be abolished by a drug, naloxone, which blocks the effects of endorphins. Benedetti induced pain in a pressure cuff on the forearm. He did this several times a day for several days, using morphine each time to control the pain. On the final day, without saying anything, he replaced the morphine with a saline solution. This still relieved the subjects' pain: a placebo effect. But when he added naloxone to the saline, and blocked the endorphins, the pain relief disappeared. Here was direct proof that the relief of pain by a placebo is carried out, at least in part, by these natural opiates.

Though scientists don't know exactly how placebos work, they have accumulated a fair bit of knowledge about how to trigger the effect. A London rheumatologist found, for example, that red dummy capsules made more effective painkillers than blue, green or yellow ones. Research on American students revealed that blue pills make better tranquillisers than pink, a colour more suitable for stimulants. Even branding can make a difference: if Aspro or Tylenol are what you like to take for a headache; their chemically identical generic equivalents may be less effective.

It matters too how the treatment is delivered. Decades ago, when the major tranquilliser chlorpromazine was being introduced, a doctor in Kansas categorised his colleagues according to whether they were keen on it, openly sceptical of its benefits, or took a let's-try-and-see attitude. His conclusion: the more enthusiastic the doctor, the better the drug performed. A recent survey by Ernst on doctors' bedside manners turned up one consistent finding: physicians who adopt a warm, friendly, reassuring manner are more effective than those whose consultations are formal and do not offer reassurance.

Warm, friendly and reassuring are precisely what alternative treatment is all about, of course. Many of the ingredients of that opening recipe — the physical contact, the generous swaths of time, the strong hints of supernormal healing power — are just the kind of thing likely to impress patients. It's hardly surprising then, that complementary practitioners are generally best at mobilising the placebo effect, says Arthur Kleinman, professor of social anthropology at Harvard University.

passageNotes.label: Paragraph 1
passageNotes.text: 想要设计一种新形式的替代医学治疗？没问题。以下是配方。作为从业者，要热情、富有同情心、令人安心且充满热忱。你的治疗应涉及身体接触，与每位患者的每次会面至少应持续半小时。鼓励患者积极参与自己的治疗，并理解他们的病症与生活其他方面的关系。告诉他们，他们自己的身体拥有真正的治愈力量。让他们付给你丰厚的报酬。用熟悉的词汇描述你的治疗，但点缀着一丝神秘主义：能量场、能量流、能量阻塞、经络、力量、气场、节奏等等。提及更早年代的知识：那些被盲目机械论科学的兴起所轻率抛弃的智慧。你可能会说，算了吧，那样的东西不可能有效，对吧？

passageNotes.label: Paragraph 2
passageNotes.text: 嗯，不，它可能有效，而且往往足以让你以此谋生。如果你足够有说服力，或者更好的是，你真正相信自己的疗法，你甚至可以过得非常好。许多疾病会自行好转，所以如果你运气好，在恰到好处的时机施行了治疗，功劳就会归你。但这只是其中一部分。一些改善确实要归功于你。不一定是因为你推荐了人参而不是洋甘菊茶，或者使用了这块水晶而非那个穴位。没有那么具体。你的治愈力量将是一种矛盾力量的产物，传统医学承认这种力量，但对此态度奇怪地矛盾：安慰剂效应。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph 3
passageNotes.text: 安慰剂是对身体没有直接作用的治疗方法，但仍然有效，因为患者相信其治愈能力。最常见的术语指的是假药丸，但它同样适用于任何器具或程序，从创可贴到水晶。安慰剂效应的存在意味着，即使是一个完全的骗子也能对某人的健康产生影响，这就是为什么一些替代医学从业者对任何提及该话题都很敏感。事实上，安慰剂是所有医疗护理（无论是正统的还是其他方式的）中一个强大的组成部分，尽管其作用常常被忽视和误解。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph 4
passageNotes.text: 在某种程度上，我们的心态能够影响我们的生理状态，这不应该令人惊讶：愤怒会使面部浅表血管扩张；悲伤会刺激泪腺。但安慰剂究竟如何发挥其医学魔力，在很大程度上仍然未知。迄今为止为数不多的研究大多集中在疼痛控制上，因为疼痛是最常见的病症之一，也适合进行实验研究。在这方面，注意力已转向内啡肽——大脑中产生的天然物质，已知有助于控制疼痛。佛罗里达大学的口腔外科医生Don Price表示，参与传递或调节疼痛冲动的任何神经化学物质也可能参与产生安慰剂反应。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph 5
passageNotes.text: 都灵大学的Fabrizio Benedetti近期的研究进一步加强了这一论点。他证明，安慰剂效应可以被一种药物——纳洛酮（naloxone）——所消除，该药物能阻断内啡肽的作用。Benedetti在前臂的压力袖带中诱发了疼痛。他在几天内每天这样做多次，每次都使用吗啡来控制疼痛。在最后一天，他没有说任何话，将吗啡换成了生理盐水。这仍然缓解了受试者的疼痛：这就是安慰剂效应。但当他在生理盐水中加入纳洛酮并阻断了内啡肽时，疼痛缓解消失了。这就是直接证据，证明安慰剂缓解疼痛至少部分是通过这些天然鸦片类物质来实现的。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph 6
passageNotes.text: 虽然科学家们并不确切知道安慰剂是如何起作用的，但他们已经积累了相当多的关于如何触发这种效应的知识。例如，一位伦敦的风湿病学家发现，红色假药丸比蓝色、绿色或黄色的假药丸能产生更有效的止痛效果。对美国学生的研究揭示，蓝色药丸比粉色药丸能产生更好的镇静效果，而粉色更适合兴奋剂。甚至品牌也能产生差异：如果你喜欢用阿司匹林（Aspro）或泰诺（Tylenol）来治疗头痛，它们化学成分相同的仿制药可能效果较差。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph 7
passageNotes.text: 治疗的施用方式也很重要。几十年前，当主要的镇静剂氯丙嗪（chlorpromazine）刚开始被引入时，堪萨斯州的一位医生根据同事们对该药的态度——热衷支持、公开怀疑其效果，还是持“试试看”的态度——对他们进行了分类。他的结论是：医生越热情，药物的效果越好。Ernst近期对医生床边态度的调查得出了一项一致的发现：采取温暖、友好、令人安心态度的医生比那些咨询过程正式且不提供安慰的医生更有效。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph 8
passageNotes.text: 温暖、友好和令人安心恰恰是替代治疗的核心所在。那开头配方中的许多要素——身体接触、充裕的时间、对超自然治愈能力的强烈暗示——正是那种可能打动患者的东西。哈佛大学社会人类学教授Arthur Kleinman说，因此互补疗法从业者通常最擅长调动安慰剂效应，这一点毫不令人意外。
